\section{Experimental setup}
\begingroup
\setlength{\parskip}{0.8em plus 0.2em}
\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}

We group our experiments into three categories.

\subsection{Category 1: predicting the fate of a seed}

Given a trained diffusion model and a seed $x_T$, we ask whether we can predict, without running
the sampler, if $x_T$ ends in a hallucination and, if not, in which mode. Our approach uses the
true score. We take points of known fate in the data space, map them back to the seed space with
the true score, and fit a predictor on the result. We then test this predictor against the fates
that the learned sampler actually produces.

\paragraph{Data.}
We use a mixture of $K$ Gaussians in $\mathbb{R}^d$, whose true score is known in closed form:
\begin{equation}
    p(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{K} \pi_i \, \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma^2 I),
\end{equation}
with $\sigma = 0.1$. Let $R_{99}$ be the radius of the ball containing $99\%$ of the mass of one component. We place the means
$\mu_i$ on a sphere of radius $2\sqrt{d/2}$, at least $3R_{99}$ apart, so that these balls never
overlap.

We consider two versions of the mixture. In the \emph{unweighted} version, all modes are equally
likely, $\pi_i = 1/K$. In the \emph{weighted} version, we draw $K$ weights from $U[0.3, 0.8]$ once
and normalise them to sum to one, and each run assigns them to the modes in a random order. The
most likely mode is then at most $8/3$ times as likely as the least likely one. The two versions
are separate experiments, each with its own trained models. The weighted version tests whether
the predictors still work when some modes attract more seeds than others.

The fate of a seed is defined by where the sampler takes it. If $x_0$ lands within $R_{99}$ of a
mean $\mu_k$, the fate of $x_T$ is mode $k$; if it lands in none of the balls, it is a
hallucination, with label $-1$.

\paragraph{Model.}
We train a residual MLP with four blocks to predict the noise (DDIM) or the velocity (flow
matching), and sample with $T_{\text{train}} = 500$ steps (Figure~\ref{fig:scorenet}). The width
is 256 for $d \le 64$ and 1024 for $d \ge 128$, since the smaller network cannot resolve the
modes in high dimension. A model that hallucinates on more than $1.5\%$ of seeds is considered
under-trained and is retrained once with $1.7\times$ the steps. Table~\ref{tab:scorenet} lists the
remaining training details.

\paragraph{Samplers.}
We study two generative processes, and for one of them four numerical solvers. All samplers are
deterministic, so each seed has exactly one fate.

\textit{DDIM.} A variance-preserving diffusion with a linear noise schedule, $\beta$ from
$10^{-4}$ to $0.02$. The network predicts the noise added to a data point, and we sample with the
deterministic DDIM update. This update is Euler's method applied to the probability-flow ODE of
the diffusion.

\textit{Flow matching.} The optimal-transport path of Lipman et al.~(2023), which moves a noise
sample $z$ to a data point $x$ along a straight line, $x_t = (1 - t)\,z + t\,x$ for
$t \in [0, 1]$, up to a small $\sigma_{\min} = 10^{-4}$. The network predicts the velocity
$x - z$, and we sample by integrating it from $t = 0$ to $t = 1$ with Euler steps.

\textit{Heun, RK45 and DPM-Solver++(2M).} These are not new models. They solve the same
probability-flow ODE with the trained DDIM network, but with a more accurate solver than DDIM's
Euler step. Heun's method is second order and uses two network evaluations per step. RK45 is a
fixed-step Dormand--Prince method, fifth order, with six evaluations per step. DPM-Solver++(2M)
(Lu et al., 2022) is a second-order multistep solver that works on the network's estimate of
$x_0$ and uses one evaluation per step. All three use the same 500-step grid as DDIM. Since they
share DDIM's network, they also share its anchors and differ only in the ground truth. Comparing
them with DDIM therefore shows how the solver alone changes the fates.

\paragraph{Anchors.}
Anchors are the training data of the predictors: seeds with a known fate. For a budget of $b$
anchors per mode, we sample $b$ points uniformly inside each $R_{99}$ ball, labelled with that
mode, and $b/2$ points in the band between $R_{99}$ and $R_{99} + 2\sigma$, labelled $-1$. We then
map all of them from $x_0$ to $x_T$ by running the sampler's ODE backwards with the true score
(for flow matching, the true velocity), using Heun's method with $T$ steps
(Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}, top).

\paragraph{Ground truth.}
We draw $50{,}000 \cdot K$ test seeds from $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and label each by running the
learned sampler (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}, bottom). Scaling with $K$ keeps the number of test
seeds per mode fixed. The anchors come from the true score while the ground truth comes from the
learned model, so a high score means that the true score predicts the learned model's behaviour.
Since $T$ enters only the anchors, the ground truth is the same for every $T$.

\paragraph{Metrics.}
We report overall accuracy over the $K + 1$ classes, mode F1 averaged over the $K$ modes, and
hallucination F1. Hallucinations make up only a few percent of seeds, so a predictor that never
predicts them still reaches high accuracy; hallucination F1 measures whether it finds them. All
results are averaged over three runs, each with new means, a new network initialisation and new
test seeds.

\paragraph{Predictors.}
We compare four predictors. Each makes a different assumption about how fates are arranged in
the seed space. Table~\ref{tab:fatenets} lists their settings.

\textit{kNN.} Assumes that nearby seeds share a fate. A seed receives the most common label among
its 10 nearest anchors.

\textit{Altered kNN.} Assumes that a hallucination is a seed whose nearest anchors come from
different modes. It therefore uses mode anchors only, and no hallucination anchors. Around each
mean, we place $b/5$ points on
each of five spheres, with radii from $0.3R_{99}$ to $1.5R_{99}$ in steps of
$0.3R_{99}$. All points carry that
mode's label, with weights decreasing linearly from $0.84$ to $0.2$, so that anchors closer to
the mean count more. As before, we map them to the seed space with the true score.

For a seed $x$, let $w_j$ and $y_j$ be the weight and label of its $j$-th nearest anchor,
$j = 1, \dots, 10$. The score of mode $c$ is
\begin{equation}
    s_c = \frac{\sum_j w_j \, [y_j = c]}{\sum_j w_j},
\end{equation}
and $p = \mathrm{softmax}(s / 0.1)$. When the neighbours agree, $p$ is concentrated on one mode;
when they disagree, it is spread out. We measure this with the confidence $1 - H(p)/\log K$,
where $H$ is the entropy. A seed whose confidence falls below a threshold $\theta$ is a
hallucination; otherwise it is assigned to the mode with the largest $p_c$.

Since the anchors contain no hallucinations, $\theta$ cannot be learned from them. Instead, we set
it on 5{,}000 separate seeds labelled with the true score: we try 100 values between the $0.5\%$
and $50\%$ quantiles of their confidence and keep the one with the highest hallucination F1.

\textit{Quadratic network.} Assumes that the boundaries between fates are quadratic surfaces. It
is a linear classifier with $K + 1$ outputs on $x$ and all products $x_i x_j$ ($i \le j$).

\textit{Polar network.} Assumes that the fate depends mainly on the direction of the seed, and that
hallucinations lie on the boundaries between modes. The first holds because seeds concentrate
near $\|x_T\| = \sqrt{d}$. We therefore write a seed as a direction $u = x / \|x\|$ and a radial
offset $r = \|x\| - \sqrt{d}$. A linear layer maps $(u, r)$ to a vector $z$ of size 256, and the
$K$ mode logits are a linear function of $z$, $z^2$ and $z^3$ (element-wise). The hallucination logit
grows as the two best modes get closer, that is, near a boundary:
\begin{equation}
    \ell_{\text{hall}} = c + a\,r - b\,(\ell_1 - \ell_2),
\end{equation}
where $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ are the two largest mode logits and $a$, $c$ and $b > 0$ are learned.

Both networks are trained with cross-entropy on all anchors, each as an ensemble of three models.
